issue_polls.stat: 35% pick inflation/prices as their most important issue, roughly triple the next-highest issues (health care and jobs/economy, 12% each)
58% of registered voters are extremely concerned about inflation; about 6 in 10 name cost of living as their top economic worry
66% call inflation a very big problem for the country, up from 63% a year earlier
In the open-ended most important problem question, 17% named inflation and 38% named some economic issue
73% say the affordability of health care is a very big problem, up 6 points from February 2025
61% worry a great deal about health care access and affordability, the highest of 16 domestic issues tested
66% worry about affording health care; 67% say Congress did the wrong thing by not extending enhanced ACA tax credits
66% say the federal government is responsible for ensuring all Americans have health coverage; 35% favor a single national government program and 31% a mix of government and private programs
74% say the role of money in politics is a very big problem, the top item of 13 tested, with majorities in both parties agreeing
60% of registered voters are extremely concerned about government corruption, the highest of 13 issues tested
81% of registered voters support banning members of Congress from trading stocks
29% think most people running the government are corrupt and another 53% think many are
50% of registered voters call the economy extremely important to their midterm vote, tied for the top of 11 issues
51% worry a great deal about the economy; 35% worry a great deal about unemployment
36% call unemployment a very big problem, up 11 points from early 2025
61% of registered voters call gas prices a major problem, up from 48% two years earlier
50% of registered voters are extremely concerned about gas prices
42% of registered voters call gas prices extremely important to their midterm vote
26% name government or leadership as the most important problem, the single most-mentioned category
64% say the ability of Democrats and Republicans to work together is a very big problem
49% of registered voters are extremely concerned about government leadership
64% say the federal budget deficit is a very big problem, up 7 points from February 2025
50% worry a great deal about federal spending and the budget deficit
15% of registered voters name government spending as their top economic worry, second to cost of living
47% of registered voters call the situation in Iran extremely important to their midterm vote, third of 11 issues
42% of registered voters are extremely concerned about the Iran war
34% say using military force in Iran was the right decision; 65% disapprove of the president's handling of the conflict
63% prefer ending the Iran war quickly even if objectives are unmet, versus 21% who prefer fighting until objectives are achieved
40% of registered voters call immigration extremely important to their midterm vote
44% mention immigration as an issue for the government to work on in 2026, down from about half the prior year
38% call illegal immigration a very big problem, down from 48% in February 2025
52% say the administration is doing too much to deport immigrants in the country illegally; 31% say about the right amount and 15% too little
78% say there is a serious threat to the future of democracy
32% of registered voters are extremely concerned about voter suppression and 28% about voter fraud
44% of registered voters call income and wealth distribution extremely important to their midterm vote
49% worry a great deal about the distribution of income and wealth
57% of registered voters say capitalism does not give people a fair shot
54% of registered voters call housing costs a major problem, down from 60% two years earlier
About 2 in 10 adults want the federal government to focus on housing costs in 2026, rising to about a quarter of those under 30
59% worry about affording prescription drugs, the highest share since KFF began asking in 2018
72% say there is too little government regulation limiting drug prices, versus 13% who say too much
55% say drug addiction is a very big problem for the country
37% worry a great deal about drug use
49% say gun violence is a very big problem for the country
56% want laws covering firearm sales made more strict, 27% kept as they are and a record-high 15% made less strict
54% favor banning the manufacture, possession and sale of semiautomatic rifles; 44% oppose
38% of registered voters call abortion extremely important to their midterm vote
60% say abortion should be legal in all or most cases, down from 63% in 2024; 55% say medication abortion should be legal
47% say violent crime is a very big problem for the country
39% worry a great deal about crime and violence, down 8 points from 2025
35% of registered voters call crime extremely important to their midterm vote

exit_national.stat: Economy was named the most important issue facing the country by 39% of voters, followed by state of democracy at 32%.
Preliminary exit polls put immigration at 14%, health care 8%, foreign policy 4% and crime 3% as most important issue (pollster not named in the write-up).
exit_national.source: Winston Group summary of preliminary exit polls

exit_national.stat: About 4 in 10 voters named the economy as top issue, roughly 3 in 10 state of democracy, and about 1 in 10 each immigration and health care.
More than 80% of voters said they were worried about prices of health care (along with gas, groceries, utilities).
Voters favored Democrats over Republicans on handling health care by 19 points, 49% to 30%, versus a 7-point Harris edge on this in 2024.
exit_national.source: KFF analysis of the 2026 Voter Poll (SSRS)

exit_national.stat: 54% said Trump administration policies made their own health care costs worse and 10% said better; those saying worse backed Democratic House candidates 82% to 16%.
exit_national.source: KFF analysis of the 2026 Voter Poll (SSRS)

exit_national.stat: 30% of voters said they support the MAHA movement, 39% do not, and 31% did not know enough.
Democrats won independents by 22 points nationally, and independents were 33% of the electorate (pollster not named in the article).
